I am an upper middle class Canadian and I have lived in both major metropolitan areas as well as tiny rural communities. From a medical care perspective this is a difference between night and day.

When I was living in a small town I had serious back problems and was unable to receive proper medical help because the local hospital's hours were so limited for non-emergency issues, and because I was unable to get time off work as I was running my own business and struggling to make ends meet. Eventually the issues sorted themselves out and I was able to move on with my life, but the medical system had failed me miserably.

More recently I have had a few other medical issues, one that required surgery and an MRI, and another that required an MRI. I was fortunate to be living in a major metropolitan centre and had access to a great family doctor, top notch hospitals and some great care. I am still receiving great care on a weekly basis, and have been for over a year.

My daughter lives about an hour outside of my city and has a condition that requires regularly scheduled checks on her heart. She and her mother (who also has this hereditary heart issue) travel to the city once a month to have a variety of tests done at a world class health centre. Her mother has recently had several emergency issues with her heart that has required a trip to the city and hospital stays.

So what does all this mean? In the city centres, access to health care is generally pretty stellar, but once you get outside of these urban areas, your quality of healthcare tends to decline rapidly.

A vast majority majority of Canada's population is located in a few large metropolitan areas and Canada is VERY big. A small part of the reason I have chosen to live where I do is because of access to great healthcare, but this is not a choice that many Canadians can make. In many smaller cities in Canada, the distance between them is great, requiring 8+ hour car rides to get from one city to another, and I cannot comment on the quality of care in these smaller cities, though I would hazard a guess that it does not match the quality and access to healthcare that I enjoy.

Canada's healthcare is very good for the majority of Canadians, but in the majority of geographic areas, it is lacking. And we do pay for dearly for it, especially if you have a good income stream on the books.

I am happy enough paying for our universal healthcare system, so that many Canadians can have access to healthcare, independent of income, but I would be happier paying into it if I knew that all Canadians would have access to that level of medical access.
